catalog_quote: It is not clear whether something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Meꞌphaa. However, there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed. Rensch (1978:631) refers to the “tonic ultima”. Suárez (1983:26) likewise gives reasons for considering that, at least at an earlier stage of the language, the final syllable was accented. Poser (1990) has provided ample evidence that a language (Japanese, in his case) may have foot structure despite not having a “stress system”. First, as we have alluded to already, various phonetic details require reference to a weak syllable of the root. In a disyllabic root, the final syllable is strong and the first is weak. ... Monosyllabic minor class words (discourse markers, subordinators) typically have the properties of weak syllables. The addition of an affix does not affect the basic prosodic structure; the root in the word continues to have a weak syllable followed by a strong one. [Marlett & Weathers 2018 §7 p. 23] ... Tones have been analyzed as being basically three (High, Mid, and Low) in all of the previous work and in the exposition of tone in the Acatepec variety [tpx] found in Cline (2013). [§6 p. 22] ... Las lenguas tlapanecas son tonales. Aparentemente todas las variedades tienen tres tonos: alto, medio y bajo. [Marlett 2018 §3 p. 5]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Las lenguas tlapanecas son tonales. Aparentemente todas las variedades tienen tres tonos: alto, medio y bajo. [...] Las oclusivas sonoras no prenasalizadas /b/ y /ɡ/ suelen pronunciarse “suavemente”, como fricativas o aproximantes, en muchas posiciones. Sin embargo, en la última sílaba de la raíz de una palabra, como en xa̱bu̱ ‘persona’, se pronuncian como oclusivas (a diferencia de lo que sucede en el español). La oclusiva dental sonora se ha convertido en una vibrante sencilla, o a veces múltiple, en sílabas no finales de la raíz y en la mayoría de contextos débiles; en estos casos, se escribe como r.
new_statements.translation: The Tlapanec languages are tonal. Apparently all the varieties have three tones: high, mid and low. [...] The non-prenasalized voiced stops /b/ and /ɡ/ are usually pronounced 'softly', as fricatives or approximants, in many positions. However, in the last syllable of the root of a word, as in xa̱bu̱ 'person', they are pronounced as stops (unlike what happens in Spanish). The voiced dental stop has become a simple, or sometimes trilled, vibrant in non-root-final syllables and in most weak contexts; in these cases it is written as r.
new_statements.citation: Marlett, Stephen A. 2018. Propuesta de convenciones para escribir el miꞌphaa de Tlacoapa. Propuestas de convenciones para escribir las lenguas originarias de México, #10. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Propuesta de convenciones para escribir el miꞌphaa de Tlacoapa', author Stephen A. Marlett, 11 pp., XLingPaper, created 2018-09-05; has a text, no scanned needed). Quote check with extracted text: §3 'Tonos' on p.5 reads exactly 'Las lenguas tlapanecas son tonales. Aparentemente todas las variedades tienen tres tonos: alto, medio y bajo. En la ortografía, se indica el tono alto con un acento agudo y el tono bajo, con una raya debajo de la vocal. El tono medio se representa con la falta de diacríticos.' §4.2 'Oclusivas sonoras' on p.6 reads exactly 'Las oclusivas sonoras no prenasalizadas /b/ y /ɡ/ suelen pronunciarse "suavemente", como fricativas o aproxi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tlacoapa Me'phaa is a three-tone language (high, mid, low). The source makes no statement about word stress or accent. It does treat the root-final syllable as the strong position (voiced stops remain stops only there; /d/ lenites to [r] in non-final root syllables and other 'weak contexts'), the same pattern that Marlett's Acatepec illustration (acat1239) describes as an iambic structure with the final syllable stronger 'although nothing precisely of the character of accent has been identified'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for tone or prominence; the consonant-allophony diagnostic has exceptions (some words keep unaspirated voiceless stops; /d/ vs [r] alternation described as 'la mayoría de contextos débiles').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/word ('la última sílaba de la raíz de una palabra'); data are isolated citation forms in an orthography proposal, not connected speech. The source is a writing-conventions paper, but its introduction says it includes phonetic and phonological details 'que no se han presentado en otros trabajos' and follows Marlett & Weathers 2018 (ms.) for the analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Marlett 2018 describes exactly the Tlacoapa town/municipality variety, ISO 639-3 tpl, Glottolog tlac1237 (autonym miꞌpha̱a̱ míŋuíí; INALI 'tlapaneco del centro'), so identity matches the target. The explicit 'iambic structure / final syllable stronger, no accent identified' wording is from the Acatepec illustration (acat1239, already in catalog) and the unpublished Marlett & Weathers ms., not from a Tlacoapa source; for tlac1237 only the tone statement and the root-final strong-syllable allophony are first-hand. Weathers 1976 and Oropeza Bruno 2014 are coded by Glottolog to Malinaltepec Me'phaa [tcf]/mali1285.

new_statements.quote: Hay varios elementos fonéticos, como la duración de la vocal en la última sílaba, que no se han analizado suficientemente y por lo tanto preferimos incluirlos en la transcripción para poder estudiarlos en el futuro. Los tonos se indican en el espacio después de la representación segmental: B para tono bajo, M para tono medio y A para tono alto. Los tonos se separan con un punto cuando están en sílabas distintas, y se juntan cuanto están en la misma sílaba. Los datos de subtiaba se presentan con convenciones diferentes dado que estamos interpretando las transcripciones de Lehmann. Se incluye un acento agudo donde lo usaba Lehmann, suponiendo que tiene que ver con un tono alto o más alto que otro.
new_statements.translation: There are various phonetic elements, such as the duration of the vowel in the last syllable, that have not been analyzed sufficiently and so we prefer to include them in the transcription in order to study them in the future. Tones are indicated in the space after the segmental representation: B for low tone, M for mid tone and A for high tone. Tones are separated with a period when they are on different syllables, and are joined when they are on the same syllable. The Subtiaba data are presented with different conventions since we are interpreting Lehmann's transcriptions. An acute accent is included where Lehmann used it, on the assumption that it has to do with a high tone or a tone higher than another.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ). The XEP text letter-spaces every word, so I re-extracted with PyMuPDF and compared whitespace-insensitively: the whole quoted passage (Hay varios elementos foneticos.. un tono alto o mas alto que otro) is on PDF page 4 = printed page 4, Introduccion, character for character. Whole-PDF term search: 'acento/acent' occurs only on p. 4 (Lehmann's acute on extinct Subtiaba, read as high tone); no stress, tonic, fuerte, debil or prominen anywhere; tone is marked B/M/A after every transcription and no stress marks appear. Identity: p. 3 lists Tlacoapa [tpl] with data from Elias Tamarit Beristrain and Emilia Neri Mendez alongside tcf, tpx, Teocuitlapa, tpc and sut; column headers on p. 5 carry '…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Marlett 2018 (Propuesta de convenciones, §3 p. 5): tonal, three tones (alto, medio, bajo), no stress statement. Adds nothing on placement; its passing remark that vowel length in the final syllable is unanalyzed is consistent with the root-final strong position noted in Marlett 2018 §4.2 but is not a stress claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work is a comparative wordlist, not a grammar. It transcribes every Meꞌphaa variety (including Tlacoapa [tpl]) with three level tones (bajo, medio, alto) and makes no statement about word stress; the only 'acento' mentioned is Lehmann's acute on extinct Subtiaba, which the authors read as high tone, not stress. The one prosodic remark is that final-syllable vowel duration is unanalyzed. No stress marks appear in any of the transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Vocabulario básico 2010 is a comparative list over Malinaltepec [tcf], Tlacoapa [tpl] (data from Elías Tamarit Beristrain and Emilia Neri Méndez), Acatepec [tpx], Azoyú [tpc], San Lucas de Teocuitlapa and extinct Subtiaba [sut]; its tone note applies to all varieties, the acute-accent remark only to Subtiaba. Marlett & Weathers 2018 is pan-Meꞌphaa with examples tagged [tpl-Tlac] (Tlacoapa) and [tpl-CGal]; the prominence claim is made for Meꞌphaa as a whole, not for Tlacoapa specifically.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ). §7 'Prominence' begins on PDF page 23 = printed page 23; the quoted passage is there verbatim except that the PDF uses curly quotation marks around 'tonic ultima' and 'stress system' where the report has straight ones. I read §7 in full (pp. 23-24) and §8.2 (p. 25): the authors decline to identify stress ('not clear whether something comparable to stress is appropriately identified'), argue words and phrases are prosodically right-headed, a disyllabic root is weak + strong (final) syllable, affixation does not change this, lexicalized phrases lose vowel length/vowels on the left, minimal-word constraint of two moras, and long vowels occur only in the strong syllable (§8.2). Earlier secti…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tone language, no stress statement record and with Marlett 2018 §4.2 (root-final syllable is the strong position); adds the explicit prominence discussion: right-headed, final syllable of the root strong, first weak, with the explicit caveat that this may be foot structure rather than stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Three-tone language (low, mid, high, with melodies). The authors decline to say a stress system exists, but state that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed: in a disyllabic root the final syllable is strong and the initial syllable weak (lenition, vowel loss and /b/>/w/, /k/>/h/ substitutions target weak syllables; long vowels occur only in the strong syllable; affixation does not change the weak+strong root structure). They cite Rensch's 'tonic ultima' and Suárez's final-syllable accent for an earlier stage. If read as stress, the placement is root-final (word-final within the root).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing; monosyllabic minor-class words (discourse markers, subordinators) behave like weak syllables
new_statements.exceptions: Statement is hedged ('not clear whether something comparable to stress is appropriately identified'); foot structure without a stress system is the analysis offered. Data are pan-Meꞌphaa (tcf, tpc, tpl, tpx) with [tpl-Tlac] and [tpl-CGal] examples, not Tlacoapa-specific.

Follows Marlett & Weathers 2018 ms. for the phonological analysis.
